newsitem.title: UK: BA shares boosted by hopes for American deal.
newsitem.headline: BA shares boosted by hopes for American deal.

text.p: Shares in British Airways took off on Monday fuelled by renewed hopes that its proposed alliance with American Airlines can get through the regulatory obstacles now that Britain has conditionally approved the deal.

BA's share price raced up 21-1/2 pence to close in London at 601 pence on Monday, shrugging off a report that the European Commission (EC) could clash with Britain in a political power struggle over who has the right to approve the deal.

"That aside I think (the terms of British approval) provide the basis for the deal to go ahead, because it appears to annoy everybody equally and also it certainly lays the ground to get past a lot of the U.S. objections," said Chris Avery, industry analyst at Paribas Capital Markets.
"I am comfortable that this (Britain's approval) is the first log moving in the logjam to get the deal done," he said.

British trade minister Ian Lang announced late on Friday that the government would clear the deal if the two airlines sold off or leased out a total of 168 weekly takeoff and landing slots at London Heathrow to new transatlantic competition.
Another analyst, who declined to be named, said any row between the EC and Britain at this stage was likely to prove a sideshow to the main issue -- getting approvals in the U.S.
He noted that the EC is not due to pronounce on the deal until next April as part of the findings of a wider investigation into all transatlantic airline alliances.
"I can't help but think that the real hurdle now is still to negotiate this thing with the United States," he said.
"They (the U.S. authorities) have a very large constituency of U.S. carriers and that's going to be a difficult audience to please," he added.

However, analysts said Britain could find it more difficult to settle terms for open skies with the United States if the European Union was seen to be objecting to the BA/American deal at the same time.
European Union sources told Reuters on Monday that the European Commission considered slot trading illegal and that it would rule on the BA/American deal itself.
"Selling slots is not something that we can accept. It's not legal," one source said. "We have our own jurisdiction and we are going to apply it."

In reaction the British government said it was surprised by the report, since it had consulted with the EC about the terms of Lang's ruling before he made his announcement on Friday and the EC had not suggested that slot trading was illegal.

"The EC was fully aware of both the content and timing of the President of the Board of Trade's (Ian Lang's) announcement," a government spokeswoman said. "The Commission has not suggested to the British government that (EU) regulations on slots might prohibit trading," she added.
